newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - MAM ups full-yr profit, new business.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - MAM ups full-yr profit, new business.

text.p: Britain's Mercury Asset Management Plc on Thursday reported a 22-percent rise in annual pre-tax profits on the back of new business gains and favourable world markets, but warned that growth may not be sustainable.
"Shareholders cannot necessarily expect these rates of growth to be sustainable in the future," MAM said in a statement accompanying results.
In an interview following the results, chairman Hugh Stevenson told Reuters the warning was intended to reflect necessary caution about the investment climate.

It had seen 20-percent-plus earnings growth over the last ten years on the back of the favourable climate for portfolio investment, but could not predict the climate over the next ten, he said, adding that there would always be a degree of caution when a new government came to power.

MAM said pre-tax profit before exceptional items rose to 171.3 million pounds ($281.4 million) for the year ended March 31 from 140.4 million previously. Its shares fell 35p to 14.065 stg by 0900 GMT, hit by the company's caution on profit growth.
In the 10 years since its flotation, Mercury's funds under management had increased to 89.7 billion pounds, representing compound annual growth of 15.4 percent.
Earnings per share had risen at a compound rate of 20.6 percent to an adjusted 63.8 pence.

Stevenson said MAM had seen continued strong growth in new business since the end of March following a record full-year performance which pulled in 5.3 billion sterling in net new business, and 3.3 billion in the second-half alone. The previous full-year record was 3.6 billion.
Stevenson said the strong new business figure had been buoyed by the UK and Japan in particular, and MAM had won a considerable number of mandates in the year.
MAM said growth also came from portfolio reorganisation fees and significantly higher performance fees as a result of investment performance achieved for clients.
While pre-tax results were in line with expectations, MAM announced a higher than expected dividend totalling 45 pence against expectations of between 41 and 42 pence.
Stevenson said the higher dividend reflected the group's push for a more liberal distribution policy.

But he said MAM's strong balance sheet, supported by a 250 million sterling loan facility it took out earlier this year, represented an appropriate level of capital and liquidity and MAM had no intention of drawing down capital through a distribution to shareholders.
It had not ruled out acquisitions to build its business, but this would not be done without considering value for shareholders, he said.

"We do not seek growth for its own sake. We do not have the resources to pursue every market and every possibility for new business. We therefore judge the opportunities open to us above all against the yardstick of profitability and we focus on the products and markets where we see particular opportunities," a statement said.

Stevenson said MAM had done well so far by growing organically. In the U.S., MAM added $1 billion in new assets with major plan sponsors, reflecting success in obtaining international specialist mandates.
The international business remained the faster growth area for MAM, but Stevenson said the UK market was not static, especially in defined contribution (DC) area.
DC business was strong in the year, with assets under management in this area topping one billion sterling.
Stevenson said it was too early to comment on possible changes by the new Labour government to Advance Corporation Tax (ACT), which pension funds have warned could undermine the industry.
"Obviously anyone can work out the arithmetic...but I think it is too early to comment until we know what the budget next month is going to hold," he said.
